questions.prompt: `numbers` is a `List<List<int>>` holding `{1,2}`, `{3,4}` and `{5,6}`. What is the difference between `numbers.Select(n => n)` and `numbers.SelectMany(n => n)`?
options: Both give the six numbers; `SelectMany` also removes duplicates
`Select` flattens the lists; `SelectMany` keeps them nested
`Select` gives a sequence of three lists; `SelectMany` gives one sequence `1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6`
`SelectMany` only works with a result selector
questions.explanation: `Select` gives you a sequence of sequences, while `SelectMany` projects each element to an `IEnumerable` and flattens the results into one sequence.
`Skip((2 - 1) * 3)` bypasses the first 3 elements and `Take(3)` returns the next 3, so page 2 is `40, 50, 60`.
With a seed, the accumulator starts at the value you provide, so the result is 10 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 19. Without a seed, the first element would be the initial value.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, when do `nums.Where(n => n % 2 == 0)` and `products.Sum(p => p.Price)` actually run?
options: `Where` runs when the result is enumerated; `Sum` runs immediately
Both run immediately when the line executes
questions.explanation: `Where` uses deferred execution and is invoked when enumerated, while aggregation operators such as `Count`, `Sum` and `Min` execute immediately.

questions.prompt: When should you use `LongCount()` instead of `Count()`?
options: When the elements are of type `long`
When the collection may contain more elements than `int.MaxValue`
When you need the count to be deferred
questions.explanation: `Count()` returns an `int`; `LongCount()` returns a 64-bit `long` for collections that may hold more than `int.MaxValue` (2,147,483,647) elements.
